_comment: The launch feed for instagram.com/rentleaks — 20 posts, one a day.
Every claim here comes from material already on the site: data.js (markets and
housing types), rentleaks-rules.js (jurisdiction rules, each with a source),
the hire-a-broker pages and the three guides. Nothing is invented, no sample
listing is shown as a real home, and no post describes who should live
somewhere — fair housing applies to organic posts exactly as it does to ads.
Edit here and re-run tools/build-ig-feed.py: it renders the images into
images/social/ig/, writes the captions to marketing/social/IG-FEED.md and
theme: night (dark) or paper (light) — alternate so the grid has rhythm.
chips: short facts that sit as pills under the headline. Keep to 4.
photo: a slug from tools/social/ig-photos.json. The picture fills the frame
under a gradient scrim; if the file isn't in images/social/photos/ yet, the
painted card is drawn instead, so the feed always renders.

posts.headline: Housing, not hotels
posts.sub: Rooms, co-living, furnished homes, 1-month-plus stays and lease-breaks — at all-in prices, in 79 markets.
posts.caption:
Somewhere to live for three months is a genuinely hard thing to find. Hotels price by the night and aren't homes. Year leases don't bend. Everything in between is a mess of screenshots and deposits paid to strangers.

RentLeaks is the in-between, done properly: private rooms, co-living buildings, furnished apartments, 1-month-plus stays and lease takeovers — 30 days minimum, never nightly — across 79 markets in the US, UK, Ireland, France, Spain, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Germany and Italy.

Every price is all-in. Link in bio.

posts.headline: All-in means all in
posts.sub: Base rent plus the utilities, wifi and cleaning the listing includes — one number, before you enquire.
posts.caption:
The cheapest listing is usually the one hiding the most.

All-in is a number you can compare: base rent plus whatever utilities, wifi and cleaning that listing includes, shown before you contact anyone. If something isn't included, it says so.

It makes the comparison boring, which is the point — you should be choosing between homes, not decoding them.

posts.headline: Whoever hires the broker pays the broker
posts.sub: In effect since 11 June 2025. A landlord's agent can't move their fee onto you.
posts.source: NYC FARE Act, Local Law 119 of 2024 — in effect 11 June 2025
posts.caption:
The rule most New York renters still haven't been told.

Since the FARE Act took effect on 11 June 2025, the person who hires the broker pays the broker. If a landlord hired an agent to list and show an apartment, that agent's fee is the landlord's cost — it can't be passed to you, and every fee you do pay has to be itemised in writing before you sign.

The one time a renter pays is when the renter hires their own agent. That's a service you choose, at a price you agree first.

Free 5-page playbook — link in bio.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline:
One month or 15%?
$2,880 apart
posts.sub: Same apartment, same agent, three ways of saying the fee. One month is about 8.33% of a year.
posts.caption:
Convert before you compare.

Broker fees get quoted three ways — months of rent, a percentage of the first year, or a flat fee — and people trade them as if they were the same thing. On a $3,600 apartment: one month is $3,600, 12% of the year is $5,184, 15% is $6,480.

Same apartment. $2,880 between the cheapest and the dearest way of saying it.

The conversion table is in the free fee-negotiation guide — link in bio.

Worked examples, not offers.

posts.headline: Name your number before anyone shows you anything
posts.sub: Set the most you'll pay. Verified licensed agents then propose at or under it — above your cap, a proposal can't even be sent.
posts.caption:
A cap turns an awkward negotiation into a simple comparison.

You decide the most you'd pay a broker — one month, a percentage, a flat fee, or nothing at all — and up to three verified licensed agents pitch at or under it. A proposal above your cap can't be sent to you at all.

No lease, no fee. Nothing owed to us, ever.

Link in bio.

posts.headline: Three steps, about two minutes of typing
posts.sub: Tell us what you need · pick your broker · sign in the app.
posts.caption:
Hiring a broker, start to finish.

1 · Tell us the area, the kind of home, the dates and your fee cap.
2 · Up to three verified agents come back with a fee and a short pitch. You compare and pick one — or none.
3 · One plain-English agreement, signed in the app before the search starts.

Every agent's licence is checked with the state before they see a single lead, and your name, email and phone stay private until you choose someone.

Link in bio.

posts.headline: What a fair broker agreement says
posts.sub: If your agreement is missing these, that's the conversation to have before you sign — not after.
posts.caption:
Save this before your next viewing.

A fair representation and fee agreement says the fee as a number in dollars — "standard" is not a number. It says the fee is owed on a signed lease and nothing else. It applies only to homes that agent introduced, with a list you both keep. It runs 90 days or less and either side can end it in writing. And it charges you nothing for homes their own brokerage represents for the landlord.

The full checklist is in the free playbook — link in bio.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: Don't sign that
posts.sub: Any one of these is enough. The last one is prohibited outright.
posts.caption:
Four things that mean you should not sign that broker agreement.

One: the fee isn't a number. "Standard" isn't a number.
Two: it locks you in for six months with no way out. Ninety days, endable in writing, is normal.
Three: money is asked for before you've seen anything. Rent and deposits go to the landlord against a signed lease — never to an agent's personal account.
Four: an apartment is available to you only if you sign with them. That one is prohibited outright.

Link in bio for the full checklist.

posts.headline: Never pay before you've seen it
posts.sub: Rent and deposits go to the landlord, against a signed lease. Never to a personal account.
chips: See it first — in person or live
posts.caption:
The single rule that prevents almost every rental scam: see the home — in person or on a live video call — before any money moves.

Rent and deposits are paid to the landlord or the management company against a signed lease. Never to an agent's personal account, never by wire transfer, gift card or crypto, and never to hold a home you haven't seen.

RentLeaks never takes a payment and will never ask you for one.

posts.headline: Application fees are capped at $20 — and mostly banned
posts.sub: Deposit: one month, maximum. A credit report you supply, dated within 30 days, has to be accepted.
posts.source: NY Real Property Law § 238-a · General Obligations Law § 7-108 (HSTPA)
posts.caption:
New York renters pay fees that the law stopped allowing in 2019.

The security deposit is capped at one month's rent. Application and move-in charges are barred, and a background or credit check can cost you no more than $20 — which you don't have to pay at all if you hand over a consumer report you already have, dated within the last 30 days.

If a landlord or agent asks for more, the correct response is to ask which statute allows it.

General information, not legal advice; rules vary by city and state.

posts.headline: Silence is consent
posts.sub: In a building of four or more units, a landlord who doesn't answer a proper sublet request in 30 days has consented.
chips: 10 days: they may ask for more
posts.source: NY Real Property Law § 226-b — sublet and assignment
posts.caption:
Breaking a New York lease is less hopeless than it feels.

In a building with four or more units, you send a proper written sublet request. The landlord has 10 days to ask for more information and 30 days from that to decide — and if they don't answer, consent is deemed given. Assignment is the harder route: it needs written consent, which can be refused without a reason, but then your remedy is release from the lease on 30 days' notice.

Lease-break posts are free on RentLeaks. Link in bio.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: The bail mobilité takes no deposit at all
posts.sub: One to ten months, non-renewable — for tenants in study, training, apprenticeship or a temporary posting.
posts.caption:
If you're moving to Paris for a few months, ask for the bail mobilité by name.

It runs one to ten months, can't be renewed, and — unusually — no deposit is permitted at all. It's limited to tenants in training, study, an apprenticeship, a professional assignment or a temporary posting, and that eligibility is captured when you apply.

We hold the rules for every market we list, so the contract type is decided before anyone signs.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: Thirty days makes it a tenancy
posts.sub: With full protection — and since July 2024, fixed terms are largely unavailable.
posts.caption:
Amsterdam is one of the strongest positions a mid-term renter can be in, and most people don't know it.

A stay of 30 days or more is a tenancy with full protection. The deposit is capped at two months. And under the good landlordship act, a letting agent working for the landlord cannot charge the tenant a fee — the same principle New York adopted five years later.

Since July 2024, fixed terms are largely unavailable, so "it's only a six-month contract" is usually not the whole story.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: Three months, not thirty days
posts.sub: The misappropriation ban is the binding constraint, and a temporary purpose has to be documented in the contract.
posts.caption:
Berlin is the market where the usual 30-day rule doesn't apply.

The Zweckentfremdungsverbot — the ban on misappropriating housing — is what actually binds, and in practice the threshold sits nearer three months than thirty days. A shorter let needs registration, and the contract has to be a Zeitmietvertrag with a documented temporary purpose.

This is why "it works in Amsterdam" is not a plan for Berlin. We keep the rules per market so a listing is written to the right regime from the start.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: The advertised rent is a ceiling
posts.sub: Accepting more than the stated rent is prohibited, and no more than one month's rent may be taken in advance.
posts.caption:
Rental bidding in London is over.

The advertised rent is now a ceiling: a landlord or agent can't accept more than the rent they stated, and no more than one month's rent may be taken in advance. Assured tenancies are periodic, with fixed terms abolished.

If you're being asked to bid up, or to pay six months up front to "strengthen" an application, that's the rule to quote.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: A season contract has to say what the season is for
posts.sub: Catalonia's seasonal and room-rental regime reaches mid-term lets, not only tourist lets — and rent caps can apply.
posts.caption:
A Barcelona mid-term let is not a tourist let, and not an ordinary tenancy either.

It's a contracte de temporada, and the temporary purpose has to be documented in the contract itself — study, work, a posting. Catalonia's seasonal and room-rental rules reach mid-term lets rather than only tourist stays, registration is required, and rent caps can apply.

A contract that doesn't say why it's seasonal is the one to ask about.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: The minimum stay changes at the city line
posts.sub: Toronto 28 days · Vancouver 30 · Montreal and Quebec City 31.
posts.caption:
Four Canadian cities, four different floors for a short stay.

Toronto is 28 days. Vancouver is 30. Montréal and Québec City are 31 — which matters more than the single day suggests, because a calendar month of 30 days doesn't clear it.

We hold the minimum for every market we list, so a stay is priced and contracted against the right one rather than the one that was true in the last city.

General information, not legal advice.

posts.headline: Posting a takeover is free
posts.sub: Remaining term, whether it's an assignment or a sublet, and what the landlord's consent needs — stated up front.
posts.caption:
Leaving a lease early is a bad week that doesn't need to become a bad year.

Posting a lease-break on RentLeaks is free. The listing shows the remaining term, whether it's an assignment or a sublet, and what consent the landlord's rules actually require in that city — because those are the three things every serious replacement asks in the first message.

Link in bio.
